replies.author: @phetindra8216
replies.text: Biased statement. I am a Lao person, I pay around maximum $6 US a month for the electricity (fan and fridge). replies.author: @phetindra8216
replies.text: @chrisperkins7331 I live in Vientiane, speaking the Lao language with Vientianese intonation. I speak fluently three European languages, one amongst them daily. I bet you hear a lot the word "Lao" but you usually drop the word which comes before it. Khon Lao, Ahan Lao, Meuang Lao, Mia Lao, Phoua Lao, etc.

replies.author: @chrisperkins7331
replies.text: @phetindra8216 Well my wife (of 18 ears) is Lao, all but 2 people in the village (of 2,000) are Lao . Every one of them is Lao, so I learnt from them.. So one of us is wrong. By the way where do you live and what language do you normly speak.

replies.author: @phetindra8216
replies.text: I am a Lao person. Speaking with foreigners in English we always say "Laos" with the S, clearly. Speaking the Lao language you can't hear the S that's because "Lao" is an adjective not a noun. Like English against England. We have Lao country (Meuang Lao), Lao food (Ahan Lao), Lao people (Khon Lao), Lao language (Phasa Lao) and so on. Listen to the TV, the word Lao as a country never stands alone, it is always Satharanarathpasathipataypasason Lao (Lao PDR). In Thailand always "Sopopo Lao". The stand alone "Lao" as a noun means "He/She". So calling my country in English "Lao" sounds weird for the Lao people, doesn't it.
